h1: College Soccer Recruiting Coach for Grades 9–12

blocks.html:
Getting the college soccer recruitment part right is the piece nobody prepares your family for. Your athlete already has people in their corner for the game itself: a club coach, a trainer, a high school program. But the recruiting part? That usually lands squarely on you. The late-night research. The emails you’re not sure you worded right. The quiet panic that maybe you’re already behind and nobody told you. It’s a second full-time job, and no one handed you the manual.

That’s the weight a soccer recruiting coach lifts off your shoulders. We don’t replace your club coach. We take on everything that happens off the field: the outreach, the film, the timeline, the coach conversations. The part that talent alone never handles on its own.

You get a soccer recruiting mentor who knows your kid by name and sits beside your family for the whole thing. No checklist handed over on day one and a “good luck” after that.

heading: The Complete Guide to College Soccer Recruiting

blocks.html: Most families start this process late, and not because they were not paying attention. Nobody hands you a manual. Club coaches are busy, the rules change, and every parent at the field has different advice. This is the whole picture in one place, written for the parent. Each section links to a full article if you want the detail.

Three things surprise most families.

Coaches recruit from film first. A college coach cannot travel to watch every athlete they are considering. Your athlete's highlight reel is the audition, and it does more work than any single game will.

Your athlete has to start the conversation. Coaches are not going to find your athlete. The families who get recruited are the ones sending emails, following up, and staying visible over months.

There are far more places to play than most families know. Division I is a small part of it. D2, D3, NAIA and junior college programs all field real teams, and several of them hand out more money to the right athlete than a D1 partial would.
The families who struggle are usually running a plan built on one level, one dream school, and the hope that being good enough will be noticed. The families who succeed run a wider search and work it consistently.

blocks.text: 2. The recruiting timeline, grade by grade

blocks.html:
The two questions we hear most: are we too late? and what should we be doing right now?

Freshman and sophomore year. Grades matter more than most families realize, because they decide which schools can admit your athlete at all. Start the highlight reel. Begin building a school list. Outreach can start now, earlier than most people think.

Junior year. The heaviest year. Outreach in volume, camps at target schools, and real conversations with coaches.

Senior year. Still wide open. Coaches fill rosters into spring and summer, and NAIA and junior college programs recruit later still. An athlete with no offers in December is not out of options.

blocks.text: 3. Where your athlete can play: D1, D2, D3, NAIA and JUCO

blocks.html:
"D1 or nothing" costs families more opportunities than anything else in recruiting.

Division I is the smallest and most competitive tier, and athletic money is usually partial rather than full.

Division II offers athletic scholarships with a more balanced schedule.

Division III offers no athletic money at all, and often ends up cheaper than a state school once academic and need-based aid land. Worth looking at properly rather than crossing off on price.

NAIA is a separate association with hundreds of schools, real scholarships, and lighter recruiting rules, which means coaches can talk to your athlete sooner and tend to answer faster.

Junior college gives an athlete two years to develop and be seen, then transfer with college film behind them. It is the route Izi took to Division I.

links.text: D1 vs D2 vs D3 vs NAIA: Where Can Your Athlete Play?

blocks.html:
Coaches are not coming to your athlete's games to find them. They come because somebody told them to.

The email does the work. Grad year, position, club and high school, GPA, and a film link. Say why that specific program. Send it from your athlete's address, in their name, not a parent's.

Follow up more than feels comfortable. Replies commonly arrive on the third or fourth attempt, after most families have given up. That persistence is what separates your athlete from the hundred identical emails in the same inbox.

Tell coaches where to find you before an event. Team, field number, jersey number, and times. A coach with twenty minutes and no field number goes to a game they can find.

blocks.html:
The single most important asset in recruiting, and the one most families get wrong.

Eight to ten clips is enough for a first reel. Cut tight, starting right as the play begins. Mark your athlete in the opening seconds with a circle or arrow, so a coach is never guessing which player to watch. Strongest clips first, because most coaches decide in the opening thirty seconds. Include technical and training clips, not only goals.

A phone and a free editing app are enough. Nobody has ever been turned down over camera quality.

links.text: How to Make a Soccer Recruiting Video Coaches Watch to the End

blocks.html:
Most families chase the athletic scholarship and discover late that the biggest number in the offer letter came from the admissions office.

Soccer money is usually split into partial awards across a roster, so full rides are rare. The number that matters is what your family pays after everything: athletic aid, academic aid, need-based aid, and outside scholarships together.

This is why grades function as a recruiting asset. An athlete who brings academic money costs a coach less of their limited athletic budget, which makes that athlete easier to sign. Coaches will tell you this directly.

What College Soccer Coaches Look For in a Recruit

blocks.html:
ID camps at schools already on your athlete's list are the highest-return spend in most budgets. Hours of direct evaluation by the staff who could recruit them.

Camps chosen for the brand name are a nice experience and not a recruiting strategy.

Showcases where nobody was told your athlete was coming are expensive tournaments. The outreach beforehand is what fills the sideline, not the entry fee.

Services that blast a profile to hundreds of coaches get treated like any mass email. Coaches respond to a specific message from an athlete who knows their program, and your athlete can send that for free.

blocks.html:
A junior we worked with went from around nine college coaches at one showcase game to around twenty-five at the next. Same player, same level. The difference was the emails sent before the second event.

One athlete sent a personal video introduction after months of standard emails produced nothing, and got a substantive reply from a major Division I program within days.

Another was pulled from a high-exposure camp by an injury and was ready to quit. We rebuilt the plan around fall camps, kept her in front of coaches through the rehab, and she came back with interest from multiple programs including a nationally known one.

Izi Murray played two years of junior college soccer, transferred to Division I, and came back from five knee surgeries to finish her career. Nobody gave her good odds.

She has been the athlete nobody was recruiting, the one starting over at a new level, and the one fighting back from an injury that could have ended it. That is why the advice here is honest rather than encouraging for its own sake, and why she will tell a family when a plan is not working.

She founded Push The Goal to give soccer families the guidance she wishes someone had given her.

heading: Common Questions About College Soccer Recruiting

items.q: When should my athlete start the recruiting process?
items.a: Earlier than most families think. Freshman and sophomore year are for grades, first film, and building a school list. Outreach can begin well before junior year.

items.q: Is my athlete too late if they are already a junior or senior?
items.a: No. Coaches fill rosters into the spring and summer, and NAIA and junior college programs recruit later still. Late is hard, not impossible.

items.q: How many schools should my athlete contact?
items.a: Far more than most families expect. A list of fifty to a hundred across several levels is normal, because a program can love your athlete and still have no room at their position that year.

items.q: Do we need to play ECNL or MLS Next to get recruited?
items.a: No. Those leagues bring exposure your athlete would otherwise create themselves with film, emails and camps. Plenty of recruited athletes come from smaller clubs.

items.q: How much do college soccer scholarships cover?
items.a: Soccer money is usually divided into partial awards, so full rides are rare. Most families reach an affordable number by combining athletic, academic and need-based aid.

items.q: What do college coaches look for besides skill?
items.a: Decision making, work rate off the ball, how an athlete responds to a mistake, how they talk to teammates and referees, and their grades.

items.q: Why are coaches not responding to my athlete's emails?
items.a: Usually because the position is filled, they are mid-season, or the email was buried. Replies commonly come on the third or fourth follow-up.
